payload.summary: The code executes command input via `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` in `app.py`, which can allow shell command injection if untrusted or insufficiently sanitized input reaches this call site.
payload.title: Command injection risk from shell-enabled subprocess execution

payload.summary: `app.py` executes `eval(expr)` on function input. If attacker-controlled data reaches this path, arbitrary Python code may be executed, creating a code injection risk.
payload.title: Unsafe eval on input enables code injection

payload.summary: A route in app.py is explicitly decorated with @csrf_exempt, which disables CSRF validation for that endpoint. This can allow cross-site request forgery against authenticated users when cookie-based authentication is in use.
payload.title: CSRF protection disabled on application route

payload.summary: A debug endpoint in app.py returns SECRET_KEY directly in the HTTP JSON response (`{"key": SECRET_KEY}`), exposing sensitive secret material to callers and creating a direct secret-disclosure risk.
payload.title: Debug endpoint leaks application secret key

payload.summary: `app.py` builds a SQL statement with Python `format()` using the `role` parameter (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE role = '{}'`). This is a direct code-level SQL injection risk because untrusted input is interpolated into SQL text instead of being parameterized.
payload.title: SQL injection via string-formatted role filter in user query

payload.summary: The application configures CORS with a wildcard origin ("*"), which permits cross-origin requests from any domain. This broad trust model can expose endpoints to unintended web origins and should be restricted to explicit trusted origins.
payload.title: Overly permissive CORS policy allows any origin

payload.summary: `app.py` decodes JWTs with `verify_signature` set to `False`, which allows attackers to forge arbitrary tokens that will be accepted as valid. This can enable authentication and authorization bypass wherever decoded token claims are trusted.
payload.title: JWT signature verification is disabled during token decoding

payload.summary: `app.py` uses `assert DEBUG, "not in debug mode"` for a security-relevant control. In Python optimized mode (e.g., `-O`), assertions are stripped, which removes this check and can allow execution without the intended protection.
payload.title: Security check implemented with assert can be bypassed in optimized runtime

payload.summary: `app.py` constructs tokens by base64-encoding the user id (`return base64.b64encode(str(uid).encode()).decode()`), which is reversible and provides no signature or encryption. An attacker can forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs, enabling authentication bypass/impersonation if this token is trusted for identity.
payload.title: Unsigned reversible token allows account impersonation

payload.summary: Security code generation uses Python's non-cryptographic PRNG via random.randint(100000, 999999) in app.py. This can make generated verification codes more predictable than cryptographically secure randomness, weakening the security of code-based verification.
payload.title: Insecure security-code generation uses non-cryptographic PRNG

payload.summary: The application entrypoint runs Flask with `debug=True` in `app.py`, which can expose the interactive debugger and detailed error information at runtime if used in a non-development environment.
payload.title: Flask application is started with debug mode enabled

payload.summary: Password hashing in app.py uses hashlib.md5(...).hexdigest(), which is cryptographically broken and allows fast offline cracking of password hashes if they are exposed. Use a password-specific slow hash (for example Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt) with a per-password salt.
payload.title: Insecure password hashing uses MD5

payload.summary: The code calls yaml.load(text) without specifying SafeLoader, which can allow unsafe deserialization of attacker-controlled YAML and may lead to arbitrary code execution.
payload.title: Unsafe YAML deserialization via yaml.load

payload.summary: The code in app.py hard-enables debug mode via DEBUG = True, creating an insecure default runtime configuration that can expose sensitive diagnostic behavior if deployed without override.

payload.summary: The application defines a SECRET_KEY directly in app.py, creating a risk that secret material is exposed through source disclosure, repository access, logs, or artifact leakage. This can weaken session and token integrity assumptions tied to Flask secret usage.

payload.summary: The code hashes tokens using SHA-1 (`hashlib.sha1(data.encode()).hexdigest()` in `app.py`), which is considered weak for security-sensitive cryptographic purposes. This can reduce resistance to collision-based attacks and is inappropriate for token-related security logic.
